content.title: About
content.content: White chili (Capsicum annuum) is a variety of hot pepper with a pale‑green, almost white skin. It has moderate heat, a fruity aroma and a slightly sweet aftertaste. White chili is used fresh, dried, pickled, and in sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from its almost colorless skin that fades as the fruit matures.
Capsaicin levels are usually lower than in red varieties, but still enough to add noticeable heat.
The pepper belongs to the nightshade family and is a close relative of sweet bell peppers.
In traditional Mexican cuisine white chili is often used in chilaquiles sauce and fish marinades.
Seeds of white chili can be saved for planting new plants.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains capsaicin
items.content: Capsaicin has antioxidant properties and may boost metabolism.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B6 and folate help nerve function and metabolism.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: One fresh pepper contains less than 30 kcal, making it a diet‑friendly addition.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Potassium and magnesium in the pepper support blood pressure regulation and muscle function.

items.title: Mucous membrane irritation
items.content: Capsaicin can cause burning sensations in the mouth and stomach, especially in large amounts.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may develop skin rash or swelling when exposed to pepper.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Capsaicin may enhance the effect of anticoagulants, so caution is advised for users of such medication.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: White chili can be eaten fresh in salads, added to soups, sauces and marinades. Dried peppers are used for powders and seasonings. To reduce heat, remove the seeds and membranes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh white chili in the refrigerator in a plastic bag for up to 1 week. Keep dried peppers in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 6 months.

content.title: About
content.content: A club sandwich is a multi‑layered sandwich typically made with toasted bread, chicken or turkey breast, ham, bacon, cheese, lettuce, tomato and mayonnaise. It is often cut into quarters and held together with a toothpick. The sandwich is a staple in restaurants and cafés worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first club sandwich appeared in the early 1920s at New York's "S. Club" restaurant.
The classic recipe uses three slices of bread, making it heartier than a regular sandwich.
In the United States the sandwich is called a "club" from "clubhouse", referring to dishes served in private clubs.
Variations include avocado, egg, tuna or vegetarian versions with grilled vegetables.
It is believed the original sandwich was created to use leftover meat and bread after dinner.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken, turkey and bacon provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and whole‑grain bread contain niacin, riboflavin and vitamin B6, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Contains vegetables
items.content: Tomato and lettuce add vitamin C, potassium and antioxidants.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Whole‑grain bread offers slow‑release glucose, helping maintain energy levels.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Bacon in moderation supplies monounsaturated fats, and olive‑oil‑based mayo adds omega‑9.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Ham, bacon and mayo can lead to excess salt intake, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Traditional bacon and mayo contain saturated fats that should be limited in heart‑related conditions.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Mayonnaise is often egg‑based and may trigger reactions in people with egg allergy.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A club sandwich is calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is usually cut into four triangular pieces and secured with a toothpick. It can be eaten by hand, though a knife and fork are also acceptable. Additional sauces such as mustard or barbecue sauce can be added to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: If prepared ahead, keep the sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. Separate the sauce and vegetables to prevent the bread from becoming soggy. Before serving, reheat the bacon and toast the bread to retain crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Cookie is a baked product made from dough, usually sweet, crisp or soft, often containing sugar, butter, eggs and various flavorings. It is popular worldwide and can include a wide range of add‑ins such as chocolate, nuts, dried fruit, spices, and more.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest cookies were baked in Persia in the 9th century.
The word “cookie” derives from the Dutch “koekje,” meaning little cake.
Chocolate chip cookies were invented in the 1930s by Ruth Wakefield in the United States.
Japan has traditional rice‑flour cookies called “mochi.”
Cookies are often used as a base for dessert bars and cheesecakes.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Cookies provide quick carbohydrates, making them a convenient snack for an energy boost.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Whole‑grain versions can supply B1, B2, and niacin.

items.title: Mineral supply
items.content: Depending on ingredients, cookies may contribute iron, magnesium, and zinc.

items.title: Mood comfort
items.content: Sweet cookies are often linked to pleasant memories and can improve mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption can lead to weight gain and increase diabetes risk.

items.title: Trans and saturated fats
items.content: Some cookies are made with margarine containing trans fats, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Common allergens in cookies include nuts, gluten, and dairy.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Savory varieties may contribute to high blood pressure if eaten in large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cookies can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, paired with tea, coffee or milk, used as layers in desserts, crumbled over ice cream, or incorporated into homemade cakes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent softening from moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: Pecans are the edible seeds of the pecan tree (Carya illinoinensis), native to North America. They have a sweet, buttery flavor and a crunchy texture. Pecans are eaten raw, roasted, and are used in baking, desserts, sauces, and as pecan butter.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pecans belong to the hickory family and are closest to walnuts.
They were domesticated by Native American tribes over 3,000 years ago.
Indigenous peoples used pecans in ceremonial rituals and as a medicinal remedy.
Pecans are rich in antioxidants, especially flavonoids and polyphenols.
The harvest season runs from September to November.

items.title: Rich in monounsaturated fats
items.content: Most of the fat in pecans is monounsaturated, which supports heart health.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains zinc and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are important for immune function and normal muscle tone.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols help combat free radicals.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: People with nut allergies may experience severe reactions to pecans.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Pecans are calorie-dense, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole pecans can pose a choking risk for young children.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Those prone to kidney stones should limit pecan intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pecans can be enjoyed as a snack, added to granola, yogurt, salads, baked goods, or made into pecan butter. They are commonly used in desserts such as pies and cookies. Unsalted pecans are the best choice for a healthy diet.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pecans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer storage keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil oxidation. Discard any nuts that smell rancid or off.

content.title: About
content.content: Green cooked peppers are mature fruits of sweet pepper that are briefly heat‑treated (blanched or boiled) after harvest. The process retains a vivid color, soft texture, and most of the vitamins while reducing bitterness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green peppers are harvested before full ripeness, making them less sweet than red or yellow varieties.
Heat treatment improves digestibility and lowers certain antinutrients.
Cooked green peppers are used worldwide in soups, stews, and salads.
Peppers belong to the Solanaceae family, along with eggplant, tomato, and potato.
Vitamin C retention is better in gently cooked peppers than in raw ones if they are not over‑cooked.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: One cup of cooked green pepper provides over 150 % of the daily vitamin C requirement, supporting immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids such as beta‑carotene and lutein protect cells from oxidative stress and promote eye health.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: 100 g of cooked green pepper contain about 20 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and normal blood pressure.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to peppers, ranging from skin rash to swelling.

items.title: Potential nitrate content
items.content: Improper storage can lead to nitrate accumulation; it is best to consume fresh, properly stored product.

items.title: Gastro‑intestinal sensitivity
items.content: People with acid reflux or gastritis may find cooked peppers irritating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked green peppers can be added to soups, stews, pasta dishes, salads, or used as a sandwich filling. They also freeze well when diced for later use.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked peppers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portioned bags – they retain flavor and nutrients for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Popcorn is a type of dried corn kernel that expands and puffs up when heated, creating a light, airy snack. Plain popcorn has a neutral flavor, crunchy texture, and low fat content. It is commonly enjoyed at movies, sporting events, and at home.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn is the only variety of corn that can "pop" due to its high internal moisture.
The first commercial popcorn appeared in the United States in the late 19th century.
In the 1940s popcorn became a staple in movie theaters when it started being sold from vending machines.
There are more than 30 popcorn varieties, differing in size, shape, and flavor.
Popcorn can be prepared in a microwave, on the stovetop, in an air popper, or in a dedicated popcorn maker.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Air‑popped popcorn without butter or sugar contains about 380 kcal per 100 g, making it a lighter snack compared with many other processed foods.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: The dietary fiber in popcorn supports digestion and helps you feel full longer.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Popcorn provides polyphenols, which help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Naturally free of gluten, popcorn is suitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Popcorn contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, important for metabolism.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Popcorn can raise blood sugar quickly, so individuals with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Added salt and oil
items.content: Large amounts of salt or oil increase calorie density and may negatively affect blood pressure.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Small pieces can pose a choking risk for young children.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to corn products, including popcorn.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Popcorn can be enjoyed plain or seasoned with salt, spices, cheese powder, or caramel. It is often mixed with nuts, dried fruit, or chocolate. For a healthier option, pop it without oil in a microwave or on a dry pan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store popcorn in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator to prevent the oils from going rancid. Discard popcorn that becomes soft, moist, or develops an off‑odor.

stewed-seasoned-ground-beef-with-potatoe.title: Stewed, seasoned, ground beef with potatoes, Mexican style

content.title: About
content.content: Stewed, seasoned, ground beef with potatoes in Mexican style is a ready‑to‑eat product that combines minced beef, boiled potatoes and traditional Mexican spices (chili, cumin, paprika). The mixture is slowly stewed, resulting in tender meat and a rich, aromatic flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mexican cuisine often pairs beef and potatoes in dishes such as carne asada and papas fritas.
Low‑temperature stewing preserves most of the nutrients from both meat and potatoes.
The spice blend typically includes ancho (ground chili), giving the dish its characteristic heat and aroma.
The product is vacuum‑packed, extending shelf life without added preservatives.
Traditionally it is served with salsa, guacamole or fresh cilantro.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef provides a complete source of protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Red meat contains highly bioavailable heme iron, supporting normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Potassium from potatoes
items.content: Potatoes supply potassium, which helps regulate fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both beef and potatoes contribute B12, B6 and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant spices
items.content: Cumin and paprika contain polyphenols that may have antioxidant effects.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Beef can contain saturated fats; individuals with high cholesterol should watch portion size.

items.title: Salt and spice level
items.content: The product may be salty and spicy; people with hypertension or spice sensitivity should adjust accordingly.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chili or cumin.

items.title: Proper heating
items.content: Improper reheating can allow bacterial growth; heat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the product in a microwave or on the stovetop until steaming hot. Serve as a main dish, with rice, corn tortillas, or use as a filling for burritos. Add fresh salsa, guacamole or grated cheese to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store refrigerated at 0–4 °C in the original vacuum pack for up to 5 days after opening. It can be frozen at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Reheat thoroughly before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Marshmallow topping is a soft, airy confection made from sugar, glucose syrup, gelatin, and flavorings, designed to sprinkle over desserts, ice cream, drinks, and baked goods. It has a sweet, slightly vanilla taste and a delicate texture that melts in the mouth.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first marshmallow recipe dates back to ancient Egypt, where they used the sap of the mallow plant.
Modern marshmallows began mass production in the United States in the early 1920s thanks to the introduction of gelatin.
Marshmallow topping is often used as a "flaming" garnish for cocktails, where the pieces are briefly set alight.
Colored versions are created by adding food‑grade dyes.
Topping is frequently sold in individually sealed packets for convenience.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: The sugar in marshmallow topping is rapidly absorbed, providing an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Easy to eat
items.content: Its soft texture makes it suitable for children and people with chewing difficulties.

items.title: Mood enhancement
items.content: Sweet flavors can stimulate serotonin production, helping improve mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar may contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Gelatin allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to gelatin used in marshmallows.

items.title: Not vegan-friendly
items.content: Traditional marshmallow topping contains animal‑derived gelatin, so vegans should choose plant‑based alternatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Marshmallow topping can be sprinkled over ice cream, yogurt, hot chocolate, pancakes, waffles, and used in baking and desserts. It can also be briefly toasted over an open flame for a caramelized flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the topping in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator to prevent softening from humidity.

turkey-thigh-cooked-skin-not-eaten.title: Turkey, thigh, cooked, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a domesticated bird, and its thigh meat is high in protein and low in fat, especially after the skin is removed. Cooked turkey thigh is commonly used in salads, soups, and quick‑prep dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey thigh meat contains more iron than chicken breast.
Turkeys were domesticated in North America over 2,000 years ago.
In the United States, turkey is the traditional centerpiece for Thanksgiving.
When boiled without skin, the fat content drops to less than 2 %.
Turkey belongs to the pheasant family, along with chickens and pheasants.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of cooked, skin‑less turkey thigh provides about 30 g of high‑quality protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Removing the skin makes the product virtually fat‑free, suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals help maintain immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Turkey provides phosphorus and a modest amount of calcium, both important for bone tissue.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bird meat.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Undercooked turkey can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; proper cooking temperatures are essential.

items.title: High sodium if salted
items.content: If the product is seasoned with salt, monitor sodium intake, especially for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skin‑less turkey thigh can be diced for salads, added to soups and stews, or used in sandwiches. It reheats quickly in the microwave or on a skillet.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in an airtight container for 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze at ‑18 °C for up to 2‑3 months.
